items.text: REMINDER

items.label: text
items.text: It is important to remember when you draw structures that C always forms four bonds and H always forms one bond. Oxygen will form two bonds and a halogen (chlorine, bromine, etc.) atom one. If you are not sure about why these atoms form this number of bonds, you need to look back at Chapter 8.

items.label: text
items.text: There are many different families of organic compounds, known as homologous series. Examples of homologous series are alkanes, alkenes, alcohols, carboxylic acids and esters. These homologous series will be discussed in more detail in later chapters.

items.label: text
items.text: A homologous series is a series of compounds with similar chemical properties because they have the same functional group. Each member differs from the next by one -CH_2-.

items.label: text
items.text: Members of a homologous series can be represented using a general formula. The first few members of the alkane series are shown in Table 22.1.

items.label: text
items.text: In the case of alkanes, if there are n carbons in a molecule, there are always 2n + 2 hydrogens. The general formula of alkanes is CH2n+2. For methane, CH4, there is 1 carbon atom in the molecule and 2 × 1 + 2 = 4 hydrogen atoms. For propane C3H8, there are 3 carbon atoms in the molecule and 2 × 3 + 2 = 8 hydrogen atoms. We can therefore work out that dodecane, which has 12 carbon atoms, will have 26 hydrogen atoms and the molecular formula C12H26-

items.label: text
items.text: Different homologous series usually have different general formulae. For example, the general formula for alkenes is CH2n and that for alcohols is CH2n+2O.

items.label: text
items.text: A functional group is an atom or a group of atoms that determine the chemical properties of a compound. All compounds in the same homologous series have the same functional group. For example, the functional group for alcohols is the -OH group and that for alkenes is C=C.

items.text: Figure 22.6 Alcohols contain the -OH functional group and alkenes contain the C=C functional group.

items.label: text
items.text: A structural formula shows how the atoms in a molecule are joined together. There are two ways of representing structural formulae: they can be drawn as a displayed formula (fullstructural formula), or they can be written out in condensed form (condensed structural formula) by omitting all the car  s  n   s -ple CH3CH2CH3. You need to be confident about using either way.

items.label: text
items.text: A displayed formula (sometimes called a full structural formula) shows all the bonds in the molecule as individual lines. You need to remember that each line represents a pair of shared electrons in a covalent bond.

items.label: text
items.text: Figure 22.7 shows a model of butane, together with its displayed formula. Notice that the way the displayed formula is drawn is different from the shape of the actual molecule. Displayed formulae are always drawn with the molecule straightened out and flattened. They do, however, show exactly how all the atoms are joined together.

items.label: list_item
items.text: Figure 22.7 Butane. The angles between neighbouring C-H bonds in butane are shown as 90° in the two-dimensional displayed formula. In reality they are about 109.5° in a tetrahedral arrangement in three dimensions, similar to the arrangement of C-C bonds in a diamond structure (see Chapter 8, page 93).
